'''Stephen Emmott''' (born 3 June 1960) is a British scientist, entrepreneur and chief scientist of Scientific.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/12bc1ee0-f6f8-11e1-9dff-00144feabdc0|title=Is it too late to save the planet?|website=Financial Times|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-08-22}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientific.london/|title=Scientific|website=www.scientific.london|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref> Emmott was named one of London's most influential scientists, and one of the most influential people in London by the Evening Standard in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.standard.co.uk/news/the1000/londons-1000-most-influential-people-2012-innovators-scientists-8289797.html|title=London's 1000 most influential people 2012: Innovators, Scientists|date=2012-11-08|website=Evening Standard|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref>

==Education==
Emmott studied at the [[University of York]], where he completed a B.Sc. in Biological Sciences (experimental psychology), graduating in 1987 with First Class honours.

He obtained a PhD in [[computational neuroscience]] from the Centre for Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience, University of Stirling in 1993, supervised by Professor Roger Watt. Having been deeply influenced and inspired by the work of [[David Marr (neuroscientist)|David Marr]] and [[David Rumelhart]], Emmott's doctoral research focused on modelling and understanding the computations the brain performs to produce vision. He chose the visual processing of text because it is the canonical example of a physical structure designed around how the brain works, rather than the other way round.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=The visual processing of text|publisher=University of Stirling|date=1993|degree=Ph.D.|first=Stephen J.|last=Emmott|hdl=1893/1837}}</ref>

==Career==
After obtaining his PhD., Emmott took up a post-doctoral scientist position at [[Bell Labs|AT&T Bell Labs]] in [[Bell Labs Holmdel Complex|Holmdel]], N.J, US, between 1993 and 1996. He worked in Nobel Laureate [[Arno Allan Penzias|Arno Penzias's]] division, undertaking research into biological-inspired computing, applied to some of the earliest medical, financial and e-commerce applications of the Internet.

Emmott returned to London in January 1997 to lead the advanced research laboratory of NCR Corp (which then owned [[teradata]]). His work and the work of his Laboratory became recognised for numerous innovations at the intersection of science, technology and finance. This included the invention of Agent-based Internet auctions,<ref>{{Cite patent|title=System and method for conducting an electronic auction over an open communications network|country=US|number=6871190|pubdate=2005-03-22|assign=[[NCR Corp.]]|inventor1-last=Seymour|inventor1-first=Mark|inventor2-last=Emmott|inventor2-first=Stephen J.}}</ref> the digital wallet<ref>{{Cite patent|title=Portable communication device|country=US|number=6424845|pubdate=2002-07-23|assign=[[NCR Corp.]]|inventor1-last=Emmott|inventor1-first=Stephen J.|inventor2-last=Woods|inventor2-first=Sarah|inventor3-last=Johnson|inventor3-first=Graham I.}}</ref> and a biologically-inspired, probabilistic method to predict the behaviour of financial markets.<ref>{{Cite patent|title=Method and apparatus to model the variables of a data set|country=US|number=6480832|pubdate=2002-11-12|assign=[[NCR Corp.]]|inventor1-last=Nakisa|inventor1-first=Ramin C.}}</ref>

=== Microsoft ===
In 2003, Emmott joined Microsoft as chief scientist, and head of computational science.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Heger|first1=M.|year=2010|title=Tech meets bio: software and technology companies have increasingly been taking a more active role in biological research: Roni Zeiger, Michael Montalto, Ajay Royyuru and Stephen Emmott|url=http://research.microsoft.com/en-us/people/semmott/nature_medicine_aug_2010.pdf|journal=Nature Medicine|volume=16|issue=8|pages=844–847|doi=10.1038/nm0810-844|pmid=20689541|s2cid=205381392}}</ref> Emmott's vision was 'to pioneer new computational methods, tools and technologies to enable new kinds of science and accelerate radical solutions to the unprecedented challenges and opportunities of our time.'

Emmott's scientific leadership created numerous scientific and technological advances. These include the new science of biological computation and 'Living Software';<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://vimeo.com/16459894|title=Programming Life: Living Software - Stephen Emmott - PICNIC '10|website=Vimeo|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lakin|first1=M. === Scientific ===
In 2019, Emmott created Scientific,<ref name=":0" /> a science and technology company.

==Public service==
From 2005 to 2010, Emmott was scientific advisor to the Chancellor of The Exchequer. He was a member of the UK Government's 10 Year Science & Innovation Framework Committee, 2004. He was appointed by the UK government Minister for Science as a trustee of the UK's National Endowment for Science, Technology & the Arts, 2008–2012. He was an adviser to the Finnish Prime Minister's Science & Innovation Strategy, 2008. Emmott is Professor of Biological Computation, University College London, and was Professor of Computational Science (visiting), [[University of Oxford]], 2007–2014.

== ''Ten Billion'' ==
Emmott is author of ''10 Billion''.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://royalcourttheatre.com/whats-on/ten-billion/|title=Ten Billion|website=Royal Court|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book|url=https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/194/194950/ten-billion/9780141976334.html|title=10 billion|last=Emmott|first=Stephen|publisher=Penguin|year=2013|isbn=978-0-14-197632-7|location=London|oclc=829960881}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hanwayfilms.com/10-billion|title=10 Billion|website=Hanway Films|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://oftv.co.uk/work/ten-billion/|title=Oxford Films - Ten Billion|website=Oxford Films|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref> It is about the climate, ecological, agricultural, resource, pollution, energy, migration and geo-political impact of a human population of ''10 Billion''.

=== Royal Court ===

''10 Billion'' began as 'a new kind of scientific lecture', delivered by Emmott, over twenty nights at London's Royal Court Theatre, directed by [[Katie Mitchell]].<ref name=":2" /> It won widespread critical acclaim. Sarah Hemming of the Financial Times described it as 'immensely, distressingly powerful' and 'one of the most disturbing evenings I've ever spent in a Theatre'.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/46eda448-d193-11e1-bb82-00144feabdc0|title=Ten Billion, Royal Court Upstairs, London|website=Financial Times|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref> The Guardian's Michael Billington stated that "what is impressive is that Professor Emmott argues his case with an implacable logic. He is quiet, humane and deeply concerned and when he says, at the end, "I think we're fucked" you have to believe him."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2012/jul/19/ten-billion-review-royal-court|title=Ten Billion – review|last=Billington|first=Michael|date=2012-07-19|work=The Guardian|access-date=2019-08-21|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> ''Ten Billion'' was named as 'Theatrical Performance of the Year' in 2012 by ''[[The Guardian]]''.

===Book===

''10 Billion'' was published as a book in 2013.<ref name=":4" />

''[[The Guardian]]''<nowiki/>'s [[John Gray (philosopher)|John Gray]] concluded that, "The shift in thinking that will be needed if we are to prepare ourselves for living in a different world begins with reading Emmott's indispensable book."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2013/jul/05/ten-billion-stephen-emmott-review|title=Population 10 Billion by Danny Dorling and Ten Billion by Stephen Emmott – review|last=Gray|first=John|date=2013-07-05|work=The Guardian|access-date=2019-08-21|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Clive Cookson of the ''[[Financial Times]]'' said the book was "a stark, simple and short warning about the coming catastrophe, which [Emmott] feels is inevitable, resulting from [the living] human population [growing from 7 to 10 billion] and over-exploitation of the world's resources."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/a7e5ba20-e7e4-11e2-9aad-00144feabdc0|title=Crowded Planet|website=Financial Times|date=12 July 2013 |access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref> In a review of ''10 Billion'' in Nature, Hania Zlotnik noted: "His slim, even terse book [presenting] his view on the "unprecedented planetary emergency we've created" — primarily examines the transformation of the global environment by human activity, a transformation that includes climate change, increasing water shortages and growing urbanization. Emmott's assessment of the capacity of people and technology to prevent the global crises that confront us is grim."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zlotnik|first=Hania|date=2013-09-04|title=Population: Crowd control|journal=Nature|volume=501|issue=7465|pages=30–31|doi=10.1038/501030a|bibcode=2013Natur.501...30Z|issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref> ''[[Kirkus Reviews]]'' analyzed the book by highlighting its portrayal of the dire consequences of human overpopulation and environmental degradation, emphasizing Emmott's authoritative background, succinct presentation, and proposed solutions while suggesting the urgency of addressing global environmental crises.<ref>{{cite web |title=TEN BILLION |url=https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/stephen-emmott/ten-billion-vintage/ |website=[[Kirkus Reviews]] |access-date=14 March 2024 |language=en |date=1 September 2013}}</ref>

On ''The Guardian''<nowiki />'s environment network, Chris Goodall called it "error-strewn, full of careless exaggeration and weak on basic science."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2013/jul/09/stephen-emmott-population-book-misanthropic|title=Stephen Emmott's 10 billion book is unscientific and misanthropic|last=Goodall|first=Chris|date=2013-07-09|work=The Guardian|access-date=2019-08-21|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

===Film===

''10 Billion'' was made into a feature-length documentary film, produced by [https://oftv.co.uk/ Oxford Film & Television]<ref name=":3" /> directed by Peter Webber. It was supported financially by [[Ingenious Media]], Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation, [[Sky Atlantic]], [[HanWay Films]] and the Roland Mouret Foundation. It premiered at London's Curzon Cinema in December 2015 and screened at cinemas worldwide. Subsequently, it premiered on [[Sky Atlantic]] in 2016.
